q: Does warm-start QAOA at p=2 (initialized from a Goemans-Williamson SDP rounding or from the Threshold_2 output) close the classical-vs-QAOA_2 gap on the (4,6)-cage PG(2,3), or does the local-view impossibility still bind at p=2?
basis: The paper's headline is a p=2, cold-start-from-|+> comparison. Warm-start QAOA (Egger et al. 2021; Tate et al. 2023) has been shown to shift the achievable expectation upward at low p on other MAX-CUT families, but the paper does not test it. If warm-start QAOA_2 still loses to Threshold_2 on the same (4,6)-cage, the paper's local-view impossibility argument (Appendix B) extends naturally. If it wins, the headline needs the qualifier 'cold-start only'.
next_steps: Reuse code/qaoa2_aer.py; add an initial layer of RY(2*theta_v) with theta_v derived from a GW SDP solution (cvxpy) on PG(2,3); optimize (gamma_1,beta_1,gamma_2,beta_2) with the RY layer fixed and then jointly. Compare to 0.7083 Threshold_2 baseline. All CPU, no new endpoints needed.

q: Does ADAPT-QAOA at effective depth 2 (2 adaptively chosen mixer operators instead of the fixed X-mixer) beat Threshold_2 on the (4,6)-cage, and if so, is this specific to the projective-plane structure or to any D=4 girth>5 graph?
basis: Zhu et al. 2022 (ADAPT-QAOA) showed that at fixed circuit-depth budget, ADAPT-QAOA beats standard QAOA on many MAX-CUT instances. If it beats Threshold_2 at depth-2-equivalent on PG(2,3), the paper's headline is depth-2-of-the-standard-mixer-only. If it does not, that is a strong extension of the paper's impossibility result.
next_steps: Implement ADAPT-QAOA operator-pool selection on 26 qubits (statevector, Aer); pool = single-qubit Y_v mixers. Cap at 2 selected mixers to match the p=2 depth. Compare best cut fraction to Threshold_2's 0.7083 on the same PG(2,3) graph.

q: How do alternative classical local algorithms --- specifically Goemans-Williamson SDP rounding (non-local, 0.878 approximation) restricted to a 2-local extraction, and Hastings 2019 chained-local linear algorithm --- rank against Threshold_2 on the (4,6)-cage and on larger random girth-6 4-regular graphs?
basis: The paper cites Hastings 2019 for Modified Threshold_2 at D in {2,3,4,5} but did not compute it side-by-side with plain Threshold_2 at D=4. Ranking the classical local family (Threshold_1, Threshold_2, Modified Threshold_2, Hastings-linear, GW-local extraction) on the same graphs would show whether Threshold_2 is the local champion or merely one of many local winners.
next_steps: Implement Hastings 2019 Sec. 4 linear 2-step algorithm (10-20 lines of numpy per Marwaha's Appendix C description). Run all four classical algorithms on Heawood, PG(2,3), and a random girth-6 4-regular graph of ~200 vertices (constructed via random-lifts). Tabulate cut-fraction rank.

q: Under a realistic hardware noise model (depolarizing + T1/T2 decoherence at IBM Falcon-class rates), how much lower does QAOA_2 on PG(2,3) drop from its noiseless 0.66773, and how does noisy QAOA_2 compare to (noise-free) Threshold_2's 0.7083?
basis: The paper's comparison is between noiseless QAOA_2 and noise-free classical. On real hardware the gap widens. Quantifying the widening on the exact (4,6)-cage tightens the practical relevance of the headline; if noisy QAOA_2 falls below 0.5+epsilon, the claim becomes 'classical wins even in the ideal quantum limit'.
next_steps: Run code/qaoa2_aer.py under AerSimulator(method='density_matrix', noise_model=<IBM Falcon>) on Heawood (D=3, 14 qubits --- PG(2,3) is 26 qubits, likely too large for density-matrix simulation on a laptop --- so use the D=3 endpoint). Sweep two-qubit-gate error 0 to 5e-3, measure QAOA_2 cut-fraction degradation, and cross with Threshold_2 = 0.7480 for the same graph. Free CPU, no external endpoint.

q: What structural graph features (spectral gap, girth-6 vs girth-7+, non-bipartite vs bipartite, tree-like radius-2 fraction) predict the size of the classical-Threshold_2-minus-QAOA_2 gap, and is there a graph family where QAOA_2 catches up?
basis: The paper proves the gap on any girth>5 D-regular graph via a tree-limit argument (Appendix B) but does not empirically span the feature space. It is currently unclear whether the ~0.04 gap at D=4 is characteristic of all D=4 girth>5 graphs or peaks for the (4,6)-cage specifically. If the gap shrinks on higher-girth or non-bipartite graphs, the paper's headline generalizes; if a family exists where QAOA_2 catches up, that is a genuinely new finding.
next_steps: Sample ~50 random 4-regular graphs at n=100..500, filter to girth in {6,7,8}, split by bipartiteness (bipartite double-covers vs random lifts). Run both algorithms (QAOA_2 restricted to the closed-form-p=2 formula using per-graph estimated tree-fraction correction; Threshold_2 Monte Carlo). Regress gap on spectral gap, bipartiteness, girth. All CPU.
